pool.q: What should you always start with when designing a service?
options: Learning about the people who will use it
pool.explain: If you don't understand who users are and what they need, you can't build the right thing.
pool.evidence: When designing a government service, always start by learning about the people who will use it.

pool.q: When should you plan user research?
options: At the start of each development phase, updating the plan as you learn
pool.explain: Research objectives change as the team learns more in each phase.
pool.evidence: You should plan user research at the start of each development phase, and regularly update your plan as you learn more about your users.

pool.q: How should research questions change after the discovery phase?
options: They should become more specific, focusing on particular user groups and parts of the service
pool.explain: Discovery questions are broad and evolve quickly.
pool.evidence: They should become more specific in later development phases

pool.q: What helps a team focus its user research on what matters most?
options: Interviewing as many people as possible
Knowing the questions to answer and the assumptions to test
pool.explain: Clear objectives keep research useful.
pool.evidence: Knowing the questions you need to answer and the assumptions you need to test will help you focus on the most important things your team needs to know.

pool.q: How long can in-depth interviews take?
pool.explain: Length depends on the subject's complexity and the number of questions.
pool.evidence: Interviews can take between 30 minutes and 2 hours

pool.q: When might you interview people in pairs or small groups?
options: When they use a service together, like family members or colleagues
pool.explain: Interviews are normally one user at a time.
pool.evidence: You can also speak to people in pairs or small groups if they use a service together

pool.q: What is contextual research?
options: Visiting people in their everyday environment to observe how they do an activity
Testing a prototype in a lab
pool.explain: Seeing people use their own equipment, with their usual distractions, reveals real needs.
pool.evidence: Contextual research means visiting people in their everyday environment (like their home, work or school) to observe how they do an activity.

pool.q: Why watch someone complete a task in their own surroundings?
options: You see their own equipment and usual distractions, which reveals what they need
It is cheaper than any other method
It removes the need for analysis
pool.explain: Lab settings hide real-world context.
pool.evidence: Watching someone complete a task in familiar surroundings with their own equipment (and usual distractions) can help you understand what they need from your service.

pool.q: Which quality do you need on a contextual research visit?
options: A fixed script you never change
Adaptability — you never know exactly what you'll find
pool.explain: Plan carefully, but expect surprises.
pool.evidence: need to be adaptable as you never know exactly what you

pool.q: Why be comfortable with silences in a user interview?
pool.explain: Resist the urge to fill every pause.
pool.evidence: Be comfortable with silences, which allow the participant to elaborate.

pool.q: Which questions should you ask a lot in interviews?
options: 'Why is that?' and 'How do you do that?'
Questions about your own product's features
pool.explain: Open questions uncover reasons and real behaviour.
pool.evidence: Ask lots of "why is that" and "how do you do that" questions

pool.q: What should you consider before interviewing a participant?
options: How the interview could harm them, and adjust your questions
How to sell them your product
pool.explain: Research ethics protect participants.
pool.evidence: Consider how the interview could harm the participant, and adjust your questions to avoid those hazards.

pool.q: What should you prepare for a stakeholder or user interview?
options: A guide of topics plus some specific back-up questions
pool.explain: Topics keep the conversation open; back-ups help if it stalls.
pool.evidence: Create a guide for yourself of some topics you'd like to ask about, and some specific questions as a back up.

pool.q: What is a risk of the 'five whys' method?
options: Repeatedly asking why can make interviewees feel frustrated or defensive
pool.explain: Use it carefully and make sure people feel heard.
pool.evidence: Sometimes asking why multiple times can cause the interviewee to feel frustrated or defensive if they don’t feel as if they are being heard.

pool.q: How do you set up the board for a hopes and fears session?
pool.explain: Participants add sticky notes to each column.
pool.evidence: create two columns labeled “Hopes” and “Fears” on a white board or large sticky pad

pool.q: Why do participants group their sticky notes as they add them?
pool.explain: Themes make the group's hopes and fears visible.
pool.evidence: Have participants group their sticky notes as they add them to the board to illustrate emerging themes.

pool.q: When should a team analyse a research session?
options: As soon as possible after each round, while it is still fresh
At the end of the project
pool.explain: Analysing together also helps the team agree what to work on next.
pool.evidence: You should do analysis as soon as you can after each round of research, while it is still fresh in people’s minds.

pool.q: When analysing research, what should each sticky note contain?
options: One observation — exactly what was seen or heard, not an interpretation
pool.explain: Separating observation from interpretation avoids bias.
pool.evidence: use a single note for each observation and write exactly what they saw or heard

pool.q: Why involve lots of people in analysing research?
options: It makes analysis slower on purpose
It helps the team make better decisions
pool.explain: The group can also agree what to work on next.
pool.evidence: Involving lots of people helps your team make better decisions.

pool.q: In affinity mapping, what do you do with the sticky notes?
options: Keep them in the order collected
pool.explain: Groups then get titles or catch phrases.
pool.evidence: Move the sticky notes into related groups.

pool.q: In the KJ method, how do participants cluster similar answers?
pool.explain: Silent clustering avoids the loudest voice dominating.
pool.evidence: Have participants cluster similar answers without discussion.

pool.q: How does a KJ session end?
options: Each person ranks their three most important clusters
pool.explain: Rankings reveal the group's shared priorities.
pool.evidence: Reiterate the question and have each person rank their three most important clusters.

pool.q: Why shouldn't placeholder personas made without research drive design decisions?
options: They take too long to write
pool.explain: Personas must come from research to represent real users.
pool.evidence: because they're effectively stereotypes, avoid using them for implementable design decisions.

pool.q: When adding a photo to a persona, what should you avoid?
options: A photo of a real person
A photo that matches the description
A photo of someone you interviewed who might be recognised
pool.explain: Protect your research participants' privacy.
pool.evidence: ideally not an image of someone you've actually interviewed and who may be recognized

pool.q: What should research-based personas be built from?
options: Research from activities like contextual inquiry and stakeholder interviews
pool.explain: Placeholder personas without research are effectively stereotypes.
pool.evidence: Gather research from earlier activities like contextual inquiry or stakeholder interviews in a way that's easy to review.

pool.q: What does an experience map show?
options: What users do, think and feel over time, from first needing a service to when they stop using it
A list of features ranked by cost
pool.explain: It covers the whole journey, including events and related services outside your own.
pool.evidence: Experience maps provide a visual representation of what users do, think and feel over time, from the point they start needing a service to when they stop using it.

pool.q: What do you need before creating an experience map?
options: The captured experiences of several users
pool.explain: Talking to a range of users reveals the whole journey.
pool.evidence: You need to capture the experience of several users before you create an experience map.

pool.q: Once you have a draft experience map, what should you do with it?
options: Move it into your team area and live with it
pool.explain: A visible map keeps the user's journey in everyone's mind.
pool.evidence: created a draft map, move it to your team area

pool.q: What does a task flow diagram typically look like?
options: A flow chart of task and decision boxes with arrows showing dependencies
pool.explain: It shows every step and decision on the way to a goal.
pool.evidence: the basic look is a flow chart of boxes for tasks and decision points and arrows showing directionality and dependencies among tasks

pool.q: Why make the flow of tasks explicit in a diagram?
options: So you can check your understanding by walking through it with users
pool.explain: Users can spot steps you missed or got wrong.
pool.evidence: so that you can check your understanding by walking through the diagram with users

pool.q: How many participants should a design studio include?
pool.explain: Mix stakeholders, users and team members.
pool.evidence: Invite between six and 12 participants

pool.q: What do groups create at the end of a design studio?
options: A design combining the best parts of each member's ideas
A list of rejected ideas only
pool.explain: Critique in small groups comes first.
pool.evidence: Ask the groups to create a design that combines the best aspects of members' individual contributions.

pool.q: Why are code prototypes better for user research than paper sketches?
options: They can be used in production
pool.explain: You must prototype and test designs before committing to build anything.
pool.evidence: Code prototypes are better for user research because they’re more realistic.

pool.q: What should headings in a user interface do?
options: Repeat the first sentence of the text
Describe the purpose of the text that follows, without being part of it
pool.explain: Clear headings help people scan and find what they need.
pool.evidence: Headings should describe the purpose of the text that follows - they should not be part of the text.

pool.q: How do people tend to read on the internet?
pool.explain: So think about alternatives before adding more words.
pool.evidence: On the internet people tend to scan rather than read

pool.q: When should you add help text to a form?
options: Only if user research shows it is needed
pool.explain: Start with simple questions first.
pool.evidence: only add help text if user research shows that you need it

pool.q: How should a service establish whether a user is eligible?
options: Show a long list of conditions
Ask questions, rather than listing conditions on the start page
Ask users to read the law
Let everyone apply and refuse later
pool.explain: Questions spare users from reading rules that don't apply to them.
pool.evidence: ask questions to establish eligibility rather than putting a long list of eligibility conditions on the start page

pool.q: In moderated usability testing, why ask participants to 'think aloud'?
options: It helps you understand what they are doing, thinking and feeling
It is required for recording consent
pool.explain: Hearing their reasoning shows why they struggle, not just where.
pool.evidence: Asking them to ‘think aloud’ as they move through the service helps you understand what they are doing, thinking and feeling.

pool.q: When is moderated usability testing most useful?
options: In alpha, beta and live, to test prototypes or the built service
pool.explain: It can also reveal problems with an existing service in discovery.
pool.evidence: is most useful in the alpha, beta and live phases

pool.q: How long do usability test sessions usually take?
pool.explain: It depends on the number and complexity of tasks.
pool.evidence: Usability test sessions usually take between 30 and 60 minutes

pool.q: How should observers contribute during a usability test?
options: Add to a rolling issues log and pass questions to the moderator
pool.explain: Observers shouldn't interrupt from the participant's point of view.
pool.evidence: Observers should contribute to a rolling issues log and relay any in-session questions to the moderator

pool.q: What can you put in front of users in a usability test?
options: A sketch, a prototype or even a competitor's product
pool.explain: Testing early and cheaply finds problems sooner.
pool.evidence: Choose something, such as a sketch, prototype

pool.q: Who should carry out a heuristic evaluation?
options: Three to five people familiar with evaluation methods
Only the developers who built it
pool.explain: They need not be designers, but should know usability best practice.
pool.evidence: Recruit a group of three to five people familiar with evaluation methods.

pool.q: Which of these is one of Nielsen's usability heuristics?
options: Use as much jargon as possible
The system should speak the user's language
pool.explain: Familiar words and concepts beat system-oriented terms.
pool.evidence: The system should speak the user's language, with words, phrases and concepts familiar to the user, rather than system-oriented terms.

pool.q: How is accessibility different from assisted digital support?
options: Assisted digital support means helping people use the online parts of a service
Accessibility only applies to printed letters
Assisted digital support is only for blind users
pool.explain: Accessibility means the service itself can be used by as many people as possible.
pool.evidence: Accessibility is different from assisted digital support , which means helping people to use the online parts of your service.

pool.q: Whose job is accessibility?
pool.explain: Everyone should know how to avoid making things inaccessible.
pool.evidence: Accessibility is not the responsibility of one person.

pool.q: When should you start thinking about accessibility?
pool.explain: Retrofitting accessibility is harder and more expensive.
pool.evidence: Think about accessibility from the start
